subject: Agriculture
title: Who Goes Hungry?
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Who Goes Hungry?.

hook.text: The world produces enough food for 10 billion people. Yet 735 million people are chronically hungry.

buildup.text: Hunger isn't caused by scarcity—it's caused by poverty, conflict, and distribution failure.

discovery.text: Most hungry people are smallholder farmers in rural areas—the very people who grow food.

twist.text: Hunger and obesity now coexist in the same countries—even the same households. It's called the double burden.

climax.text: Climate change could push 130 million more people into hunger by 2050 by reducing crop yields in the tropics.

punchline.text: We have the food. We lack the fairness to share it.

quiz.question: How many people are chronically hungry despite global food surplus?

details.summary: Despite producing enough food for everyone, over 700 million people go hungry. This topic examines who suffers from hunger, why it persists amid abundance, and the political, economic, and geographic factors that determine who eats and who does not.
details.whyItMatters: Hunger is a distribution and poverty problem, not a production problem. Understanding who goes hungry and why is essential for designing effective solutions.
takeaways: The world produces enough calories to feed 10 billion but 700+ million go hungry
Most of the world's hungry people are smallholder farmers and rural laborers
Conflict is the leading driver of acute hunger in the world today

faq.question: If the world produces enough food, why do people still go hungry?
faq.answer: Hunger persists because of poverty, conflict, inequality, and distribution failures—not insufficient production. People go hungry when they cannot afford food, when conflict disrupts supply, or when economic systems exclude them from food access.

faq.question: Which populations are most affected by chronic hunger?
faq.answer: Rural smallholder farmers, pastoralists, landless laborers, and urban slum dwellers in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia are most affected. Women and children bear disproportionate consequences including stunted growth and maternal death.
